# Super Metroid — C# port

Title screen
Opening cinematic

Ceres Station
Ridley battle

Ceres escape
Draygon Grapple Beam kill

Maridia
Exploring underwater

Norfair
Lower Norfair
The recomp is fully playable from beginning to end. Only minor known glitches remain. ## How to set up and play You need your own **Super Metroid Japan/USA NTSC v1.0 ROM** (`.smc` or `.sfc`). ROMs and extracted game assets are not included in the downloads or this repository. The app checks your ROM, copies it into application storage, and extracts the required audio automatically. Your original file is kept. ### Windows 1. Open [Releases](https://github.com/MrJackSpade/SuperMetroidDecomp/releases) and download **SuperMetroid-windows-x64.zip**. 2. Extract the entire ZIP into a folder. 3. Run **SuperMetroid.Game.exe**. The download includes the .NET runtime; no separate installation is needed. 4. Click **Choose ROM** and select your ROM. Once setup finishes, the game starts. Later launches use the installed copy. Game data, settings, saves, and recordings live under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SuperMetroid`. Keep the extracted application files together when moving the app or installing an update. ### Android 1. Open [Releases](https://github.com/MrJackSpade/SuperMetroidDecomp/releases) on your device and download **SuperMetroid-android-arm64.apk**. 2. Install the APK. If Android asks, allow your browser or file manager to install apps. 3. Open **Super Metroid C# Testing**, tap **Choose ROM**, and select your ROM through the file picker. 4. Wait for extraction to finish, then play using your handheld's controls or a connected controller. The Android build targets **ARM64 devices running Android 8.0 or newer** and has been tested on the **Retroid Pocket Classic**, including ROM import and audio playback. It keeps its ROM copy and saves in app-private storage. Install new APKs over the existing app to keep your data; uninstalling the app or clearing its storage removes that data. ### Controls and saves On Windows, use a gamepad or these default keyboard controls: | Action | Keyboard | | --- | --- | | Move / aim | Arrow keys | | Jump / confirm | `Space` or `X` | | Dash / cancel | `Z` | | Fire | `S` | | Cancel selected item | `A` | | Aim up / down | `Q` / `W` | | Start / pause | `Enter` | | Select item | `Shift` | Use the game's save stations or gunship for normal saves. The desktop toolbar also provides debugger save-state slots. On Android, press **Back/Mode** or long-press the game surface to open **Testing tools**, including save states, settings, and controller bindings. Setup accepts both the unheadered 3 MiB ROM and a copy with a 512-byte copier header. ZIP archives, PAL images, other revisions, and patched ROMs are not supported. See [ROM setup and storage](csharp/ROM-SETUP.md) for the expected ROM hash, command-line installation, and recovery details. For help, release announcements, and playtesting discussion, [join Discord](https://discord.gg/N2W9pE7qWM). Report bugs through [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/MrJackSpade/SuperMetroidDecomp/issues), including your platform, release version, and steps to reproduce the problem. ## About the project This project translates Super Metroid's original program into readable, heavily commented C#. It aims to preserve the cartridge's behavior while making the game's systems easier to inspect, debug, and understand. The original ROM supplies the graphics, room data, tables, and audio resources used by the translated code. The Windows and Android applications share the same managed game core. Windows uses a Direct3D11 renderer with a software fallback; Android uses the software renderer. Music and sound effects run through a managed C# audio engine, with resources extracted from the player's ROM during setup. **The recomp is fully playable end to end, from the opening through the ending.** Movement, combat, enemies, bosses, rooms, menus, saving, rendering, and audio are all implemented. Minor known glitches and differences from the original game remain, so playtesting reports are welcome. ### Development and references Start with the [developer guide](csharp/README.md) for build requirements, runnable projects, controls, diagnostics, and verification commands. Additional documentation: - [Desktop renderer build requirements](csharp/D3D11_BUILD.md) - [Android builds and testing](csharp/ANDROID-TESTING.md) - [Shared ROM extraction and installation](csharp/ROM-SETUP.md) - [Tagged releases and Discord announcements](docs/releases.md) Translation and diagnostics cross-check the original cartridge against these references: - [InsaneFirebat's annotated disassembly](https://github.com/InsaneFirebat/sm_disassembly), pinned to `362be646929cf8e483f692b73a6561cfc2dc1d0d`. - [snesrev's native C reconstruction](https://github.com/snesrev/sm), pinned to `578f90b3cc49557bb70060ad033bb90b8cf8ac50`. - [Patrick Johnston's bank reference](https://patrickjohnston.org/bank/index.html). Original addresses, data tables, ordering, and side effects guide the translation. Reference annotations support diagnosis; reproduced behavior and regression tests are used to check the implementation against the supported ROM revision.

# Bokura no Kazoku decomp

<!-- status:begin -->
![functions](https://img.shields.io/badge/functions-6378%2F7223-blue) ![bytes](https://img.shields.io/badge/bytes-49.6%25-orange) ![build](https://img.shields.io/badge/build-byte--for--byte-brightgreen)

Progress, 2026-10-16 (functions in C; the rest is still INCLUDE_ASM):

| | Progress | |
|---|---|---|
| **Functions** | `██████████████████████░░░` | 6,378 / 7,223 (88.3%) |
| **Code bytes** (`.text`, 1.70 MB) | `████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░` | 842.7 KB / 1700.4 KB (49.6%) |
|   Game code, C++ units (954 KB, classes found from vtables and RTTI) | `██████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░` | 1,976 / 2,303 functions, 39.8% of bytes |
|   Game code, C-style units (378 KB, CAppMain on: renderer, files, sound, IOP) | `█████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░` | 1,946 / 2,264 functions, 51.5% of bytes |
|   dklib engine library (254 KB, heap, tasks, resources, scripts; part Sony SDK) | `████████████████░░░░░░░░░` | 1,311 / 1,483 functions, 64.9% of bytes |
|   Libraries (113 KB, libgcc, newlib, Sony SDK, linkonce code) | `███████████████████████░░` | 1,145 / 1,169 functions, 91.0% of bytes |
| Stuck ([HARD.md](HARD.md), with their exact diffs) | | 843 |

Build: Sony EE-GCC 2.96 for the game; parts of dklib and the Sony SDK were built with older
SDK compilers (ee-gcc 2.9-991111 and -01), set per unit ([docs/compiler.md](docs/compiler.md)).
<!-- status:end -->

Target: **Bokura no Kazoku - My Family Growing Up in the 21st Century (Japan)**,
Redump dump. PS2 (Emotion Engine, MIPS R5900).

## Disc image

Check your dump against these (Redump's formats plus SHA-256); `setup.sh` itself verifies the boot executable it extracts:

| File | Size | CRC32 | MD5 | SHA-1 | SHA-256 |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Bokura no Kazoku - My Family Growing Up in the 21st Century (Japan).iso` | 2,091,941,888 | `9d389b7c` | `ab2edd392d190f21b2112d67219d4ea5` | `f2a8187457148a66fbbb3841032fe430cb5572d4` | `b9b5d3a131bfd6fab9a718b5875e504e014cc52287db9d68d44947e930ae9fca` |

The boot executable inside it, `SCPS_150.88`: SHA-1 `621ffd58de52794eaa3d33885ba1288f36e19365`.

## Disc (recon, 2026-10-13)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Serial / boot ELF | `SCPS_150.88` (SYSTEM.CNF: `cdrom0:\SCPS_150.88;1`, VER 1.00, NTSC) |
| ISO | 2,091,941,888 bytes, SHA-1 `f2a8187457148a66fbbb3841032fe430cb5572d4` (check against Redump) |
| ELF | 2,018,020 bytes, SHA-1 `621ffd58de52794eaa3d33885ba1288f36e19365`, statically linked, stripped |
| Built | 2005-01-28 (file dates) |
| SDK | 2.8 era (`MODULES/IOPRP280.IMG`), Sony libraries (libsd, libmc, libpad, libmtap, libmpeg, libgraph) |
| Language | C++: GCC 2.9x name mangling (`t6TArray3Z14CSceneCharaSeti_16_Z...`), `.eh_frame` + `.gcc_except_table` |
| Compiler | Sony EE-GCC 2.96 (`2.96-ee-001003-1`), `-O2 -G0 -fno-strict-aliasing -fno-exceptions`, `as -g` for the C++ units and dklib; the C-style units without `as -g`; parts of dklib and the Sony SDK with ee-gcc 2.9-991111 / 2.9-991111-01 (docs/compiler.md) |
| VU code | `.vutext` / `.vudata` (VU microcode, `dvp-as`): stays assembly |
| Game data | `DATA/*.XAP` archives (MAP 140 MB, CHR 86 MB, ENV 33 MB, MENU 18 MB, ...) |

ELF sections: `.text` from 0x100000 (about 1.6 MB of code), `.data`, `.rodata`,
`.sbss`, `.bss`. No debug info left (`.mdebug.eabi64` is empty); worth a ccc
`stdump` pass anyway, and on any other ELF/IRX.

## Environment

`bokura-env` from [decomp-nix](https://github.com/conor-sometimes/decomp-nix):
[projects/bokura-no-kazoku/default.nix](https://github.com/conor-sometimes/decomp-nix/blob/main/projects/bokura-no-kazoku/default.nix),
built on the shared [lib/mkDecompEnv.nix](https://github.com/conor-sometimes/decomp-nix/blob/main/lib/mkDecompEnv.nix):
an FHS environment with gcc multilib, Python and the permuter's packages. Builds run on hokkaido.
Recon came from the `decomp-recon` skill.

## Build

You need your own disc image; nothing from it is committed.

```sh
.bokura-env/bin/bokura-env -c './setup.sh path/to/bokura.iso'   # venv, ELF from the ISO (SHA-1 checked)
.bokura-env/bin/bokura-env -c 'make -j'                          # split, assemble, link, compare
```

`make` ends with `OK: build/SCPS_150.88 matches (...)` or a `FAIL:` line. Python tools are pinned
in `requirements.txt`; the R5900 binutils (decompals v0.10) come from bokura-env. The flat image
from the linker is wrapped in the retail ELF container by `scripts/mkelf.py` (header values from
`readelf -lS`).

## Two builds

1. **Matching**: rebuilds the main ELF byte-for-byte. The reference.
2. **Mod**: shiftable build from the same sources for tweaks.

## Roadmap

Where this is going, in order. Phases overlap; each builds on the one before. Milestones and
their done-signals are tracked in GOALS.md.

1. **Matching decompilation** (in progress, see the status above). Every function as C that
   rebuilds the original executable byte for byte. The whole of `.text` after crt0 is already
   split into source units; what is left is the large game code (menus and screens built on the
   `state.h` state machines, draw routines, minigames), units whose data still comes from
   assembly, and a tail of stuck functions recorded in HARD.md with their exact diffs.
2. **Mod build.** The same sources built without the byte-for-byte constraint: every pointer a
   symbol, so code and data can grow and move. Needs most functions in C and the data
   (vtables, .rodata, tables) described in C, not complete matching. This is the base for
   everything below.
3. **English translation patch.** Groundwork is done: all ~9,400 strings (~280k Japanese
   characters) are mapped, `tools/strings.py` extracts them per file for line-by-line
   translation, and translations are kept in `translation/en/` without any Japanese
   ([docs/translation.md](docs/translation.md)). The dialogue lives in plain-text message files
   that scripts look up by label, so English can be any length. Still needed:
   - an archive repacker (`tools/xap.py` extracts; it doesn't rebuild yet);
   - a font check (Latin glyphs, glyph widths, how the renderer advances) and a fix if needed;
   - message window widths and a re-wrap rule; vertical-text windows switched to horizontal;
   - textures with drawn-in Japanese, edited;
   - the ISO rebuilt with the patched archives;
   - then the translation itself, file by file, with a shared glossary.
   The patch ships as a delta against the user's own disc, never as game data.
4. **Native PC port** (long term). With the game logic in C, it can be compiled for a PC instead
   of the PS2, with the hardware layers replaced: the GS/VIF/VU graphics path by a modern
   renderer, the SPU2/IOP sound and file I/O by host equivalents, pads by SDL. The Sony SDK
   code (already isolated in its own units) is exactly what a port swaps out. Prior art: the
   PS1/N64/PS2 decomps that grew PC ports. Requires the mod build first, and likely widescreen
   and higher resolution as early wins.

Like the decomp itself, none of this ships game code or assets: every build and patch starts
from your own disc.

## Lessons learned

Project gotchas live in [docs/lessons.md](docs/lessons.md): read it before matching, and add to it
whenever something here takes more than a few minutes to figure out.

## Licence

Our code (sources, scripts, tooling) is licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0 or later (see [LICENSE](LICENSE)). The game itself, and anything extracted from the disc, belongs to its owners and is never part of this repository: you supply your own copy.

# White Knight Chronicles II native-port research

Target: USA BLUS30784, disc version 01.00. The goal is native Windows execution
using static C/C++ recompilation, followed by Apple Silicon portability testing.

**This is not a playable port yet.** Analysis, compilation, boot, rendering and
gameplay are distinct milestones. Passing an analysis or build step does not
establish that the game works.

See [build instructions](docs/BUILD.md) and [contribution workflow](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md).
The [findings log](docs/FINDINGS.md) tracks verified results, open issues and next steps.

## Update 1.01 and DLC plans

We will add support for the USA **1.01 update and DLC** as part of this port.
Development currently uses the original BLUS30784 v01.00 disc executable as its
baseline, with gameplay testing starting in White Knight Chronicles I.

The supplied update's metadata confirms BLUS30784, APP_VER 01.01. A matching USA
DLC package has also been identified. Integration will cover the updated
executable and patch data, DLC discovery/loading, and gameplay/save compatibility.
**Update 1.01 and DLC are planned work; runtime support is not yet verified.**
We will also compare the European DLC for content absent from the USA package
and investigate compatibility with BLUS30784. Initial file comparison finds one
EU-only entry; what it unlocks and whether it works in the USA build are unverified.
The Japanese game, DLC and ten update packages are available for future research.
The long-term goal is to bring **all Japanese-exclusive content into the port
with English translations**, and offer **optional Japanese voiceovers**.
Content differences, translations and cross-region integration still need
investigation and validation. 

## Progress gallery

The title menu now renders with New Game, Continue and Options over an animated
background. LPCM startup logos and AC-3 title/attract movies play through the native
movie pipeline. See the [newest-first gallery](docs/GALLERY.md).
Controller input opens New Game and selects White Knight Chronicles I. Description
and dialog text now render correctly. WKC1 loading passes the guard-registration
failure and dispatches previously skipped geometry jobs. A native binding for the
standard SPURS processor-ID query prevents those jobs from reading executable
bytes as kernel data. Loading advances to a further animation program, now lifted
and observed dispatching and returning. Fixing vertex-shader cache identities now
reveals the **Customize Avatar** screen. Correcting indexed triangle strips and
primitive restart now renders the **3D room with normal depth testing**. Some
avatar pieces appeared first; correcting SPU extended-range FNMS arithmetic now
reveals the **avatar body geometry**, including arms, hands, trousers and boots.
Correcting packed vertex normals and fragment source-range modifiers now also
restores **face shading and textured clothing**. Full visual fidelity, completed
character creation, gameplay and save/load remain unverified.

[![Native avatar with face shading and textured clothing](verification/screenshots/2026-10-16-native-avatar-shading.png)](docs/GALLERY.md)

## Workspace layout

The source project is here. Private game files, generated game code, build
directories, downloaded tools and dependency checkouts live under a separate
private workspace's `work/` directory. Original game files and generated game code
are kept there; reviewed screenshots are published separately in the gallery.

The port uses the [PS3Recomp SDK](https://github.com/sp00nznet/ps3recomp).
Its pinned revision is recorded in `project.json`; its license is retained in
`LICENSE.ps3recomp`. Runtime changes must be
recorded as patches rather than silently updating that revision.

## Analysis

Using a Python environment with the SDK requirements installed:

```text
python tools/analyze.py --sdk <ps3recomp-checkout> --elf <EBOOT.elf> --output <analysis-directory>
```

This runs the SDK loader, bounds candidate functions to executable sections,
resolves firmware import names and inventories generated HLE handlers. The
coverage report distinguishes handler presence from verified implementation.

## Milestones

- Disc metadata and executable identified: complete.
- Retail SELF decrypted locally using RPCS3 CLI: complete.
- Function/import/SPU inventory: initial pass complete (56,580 lifted PPU functions;
  five embedded SPU ELFs, 12 executable-backed raw SPURS jobs and five observed
  asset-backed jobs; 22 registered SPU images).
- Native executable build: passes on Windows using the pinned SDK, Clang 23.1.3,
  local Windows SDK/MSVC headers and DirectX-Headers. `tools/build.ps1` reproduces
  the build from this workspace's prepared inputs; `-Regenerate` also runs the lift.
- Native startup: executes the game, its SPU tasks/jobs, filesystem operations,
  graphics initialization and audio initialization. GPU readback confirms the
  language-selection screen, copyright page and warning screen render natively.
- Initial UI input: a simulated CROSS press selects English and the screen fades
  into the next startup stage. Further input and gameplay remain under test.
- Title screen and menu input: verified on Windows.
- Readable New Game and WKC1 selection dialogs: verified on Windows.
- WKC1 avatar-customization UI: renders and dismisses its introductory notice;
  the default male character is visible with face shading and textured clothing.
  Full visual fidelity and completed character creation remain unverified.
- Scene, combat and save/load verification: pending.
- Apple Silicon build and testing: pending.
- GeoNet compatibility: separate later research; not established.

## Current investigation

The first native run spun on invalid FIOS conditions. `lwcond.cpp` corrects the
8-byte guest layout and implements waits/signals with portable C++ synchronization.
Its regression test checks adjacent memory, timeout/reacquisition and a real wakeup.

The runtime patches fix Windows offsets above 2 GB, reject partial SDAT caches,
avoid duplicate synthetic completions after real SPU events, and make job-chain
shutdown/join wait for actual walker termination. They also implement syscall
350 (allocation from a memory container), track container capacity and frees,
correct the container-size query ABI, and accept heap-backed SPU job binaries
instead of rejecting every binary above 0x10000000. Changes stay in `patches/` and
are applied idempotently by the build script.

`tools/prepare_sdat.py` prepares the three large disc archives with accelerated
AES and authenticates every block. It writes atomic caches beside the extracted
files; the original ISO is unchanged.

The pool-28 allocation failure is resolved: the runtime previously acknowledged
syscall 350 without allocating its requested 24 MB. The settings file now loads
and initialization advances. Both the lightweight-condition and memory-container
regression tests pass.

`lfqueue.cpp` implements import 0x8A85674D (`_cellSpursLFQueuePushBody`) and the
guest queue initializer used by WKC2. It serializes producers with the SPU atomic
line lock, publishes copied ring entries, and signals registered task waiters.
The queue regression test covers capacity, sequence wrap, waiter routing and
guest layout. All three regression tests pass.

Eight real asset blocks decoded by the lifted SPU match independent Python zlib
raw-DEFLATE output byte for byte (256 bytes and seven 64 KB blocks). The hashes
and validation method are in `decompression-verification.json`; private game
bytes remain under `work/`. Temporary SPU capture instrumentation was removed.

The heap-binary fix exposed two asset-backed jobs (fingerprints
687D4BB18564813A, 54,544 bytes; 164B23483A68CBEA, 1,968 bytes). Both have now
been lifted and execute natively. The renderer worker passes its previous wait.
`tools/import_spu_misses.py` validates newly dumped job fingerprints and wraps
them in private ELF inputs for `build_spu_workloads.py`. Prepared image inputs,
including these asset-backed captures, remain under `work/` for regeneration.

The D3D12 fragment path now binds all 16 RSX texture/sampler units. WKC2's UI
shader uses units 4 and 7; the old four-unit root signature rejected its pipeline.
It also uses the current buffered-constant decompiler API, snapshots exact inline
constant bits for each draw, honors the export-width control, and uses the API's
cubemap, alpha-test and unnormalized-coordinate handling. The shader cache includes
the static alpha comparison and coordinate dimensions. The old screen-size texture
substitution heuristic is opt-in (`SCREEN_AS_TEX=1`); it replaced real render-target
textures with a black previous-frame copy during WKC2 startup.

The runner consumes each pending flip once, removing a duplicate presentation
path. A 120-second probe observed 6,171 guest flips and 6,171 presentation calls.
GPU readback, rather than those counters, establishes the visible UI milestone.
Original GPU captures are retained in the private workspace. The gallery publishes
lossless PNG versions with optional metadata removed, alongside verification notes.

Queue creation publishes its host wait primitives before the queue becomes active,
and SPURS completion sends hold table ownership through enqueue, avoiding the
observed send-versus-create crash. A fourth regression test concurrently sends
while creating/destroying the same queue ID 2,000 times, then checks capacity and
payload order.

The FIFO walker preserves self-jumps while the SPU command producer fills its
segment. Previously it skipped to PUT and discarded commands and completion labels;
that caused a graphics-fence stall after language selection. Intentional producer
and semaphore waits are excluded from the stalled-GET recovery heuristic. SPURS
guard waits now last until notification or shutdown instead of killing an idle
chain after 20 seconds.

The later startup stall was traced to a dropped installation request: a background
check was still pending when the request arrived. `tools/apply_port_hooks.py`
installs synchronization before the original guest request. The guest then performs
the actual installation and starts loading the first logo movie. All three large
installed archives (4,364,470,879 bytes total) match their disc data by SHA-256;
see `verification/installation.json`.

The nine imported PAMF reader APIs now use the guest ABI, big-endian output and
actual stream descriptors. A fifth regression check covers synthetic video/audio
headers, 64-bit sizes, copied readers and invalid input. An optional private fixture
parses the first logo's two streams and 1280x720 video. Native startup now passes
reader initialization and reaches movie demux/decoder threads.

`dmux.cpp` now supplies memory queries, real MPEG program-stream/access-unit
parsing, guest callbacks, AU lifetimes and queue backpressure. Independent decoding
matches every pixel in 3,806 extracted video frames across the logo and opening
movie; extracted AC-3 also decodes. See [verification](verification/movie-demux.json).
The native guest receives actual video and LPCM units through its decoder calls.
Callback stacks are isolated across host threads and nesting.

The imported video-postprocessor interface now has correct guest fields and actual
progressive YUV conversion, cropping and bilinear resizing. The build enables the
SDK's FFmpeg decoder with pinned 8.1 headers and a separately supplied matching
library. A 210-frame decoder check matches every frame through the guest video API
on two sequence passes, including reordering and corruption/drop negative controls.
Twenty checks pass. The title screen and its menu render natively; see the gallery.

Packed A4R4G4B4 font textures were excluded by the D3D12 binding filter, leaving
previous artwork selected for text draws. The backend now records the current
texture, decodes through the shared RSX format/row-pitch path and creates the SRV
with the uploaded resource's format. New Game description and confirmation text
are readable. The suite also runs the SDK's texture layout, packed-format and
component-remap checks.

White Knight Chronicles I is the starting point for gameplay validation. The old
32-entry guard table filled while the game created several guards per live chain.
An unknown guard then let an unprepared job run. Guards now use allocated entries,
notifications/reset/waits are synchronized, and joining releases their owning
chain's entries. Unknown guards stop before dispatch. Regression checks cover
100 chain lifetimes and 128 simultaneous guards. The native run passes that
failure. A further 11,856-byte SPU program has been statically translated, and
eight targeted native dispatches return successfully. Ordered job-list execution
also reaches geometry work previously omitted by the SDK. The standard SPURS
processor-ID query now reads native handoff metadata, preserving job code at the
kernel's original local-store address. Loading advances to another 16,912-byte
animation program; eight dispatch/return pairs have been observed after lifting
it. FIFO consumption continues through a later timeout. A subsequent vertex-shader
cache fix reveals avatar-customization menus; model rendering and job-output
correctness still need investigation.
Gameplay, save/load and missing imports remain open.

Run `tools/probe.ps1 -Seconds 15` for a bounded diagnostic attempt. Logs and a
result JSON go into `work/probes/`; unrecognized SPU jobs go into the private
analysis directory. Probes record the last observed guest flip and presented-frame
counts every five seconds; these counters alone do not verify visible content.
`-CaptureFrames` saves four backend BMP readbacks by default in a private probe
subdirectory. `-CaptureFrameCount`, `-CaptureEvery` and `-CaptureSkip` select a
longer sampling interval; probes accept durations up to 600 seconds, with each
host wait bounded to five seconds. `PAD_SCRIPT` can supply timed controller pulses
through the SDK's controller path; the probe records that script in its result.
Capture suppresses the runner's pre-flip placeholder presents, changing
presentation timing for diagnostics. `WKC2_THREADS=1` adds guest thread register
snapshots at each progress report.
`tools/trace_calls.py` optionally adds opt-in return/argument
tracing to selected generated functions. Those diagnostics are disabled unless
`WKC2_TRACE_CALLS=1` is set.

# hyperblade-decomp

A byte-matching decompilation of `HYPERX.EXE` v1.0.0.1, from the 1996 game HyperBlade, built with Visual C++ 6.0 SP3 and scored per function by [reccmp](https://github.com/isledecomp/reccmp). Its method and tooling follow the [LEGO Island decompilation](https://github.com/isledecomp/isle). This repository has a basic bring-up shim that gets the game running in its simplest form, for testing; see [Running the game](#running-the-game). To play on a modern system, use [hyperblade-20XX](https://github.com/zach2good/hyperblade-20XX), the modernised and portable version of this project. You need your own copy of the game. The logo and screenshot are shown for identification. Not affiliated with Activision or WizBang! Software Productions.

## Status

**2,791 of 3,054 game functions match exactly: 473,691 bytes, 75.34 per cent of game code.** | Measure | Value | | --- | --- | | Game functions, below `0x004a0000` | 3,054 | | **Matching exactly** | **2,791** | | Effective but not exact | 29 | | Exact bytes of game code | 473,691 of 628,779 | | Rows in `symbols/functions.csv`, the C runtime included | 4,121 | ## Requirements - Windows. Run the commands below from Git Bash, which also provides `patch`. - CMake 3.21 or later, for the presets. - Python 3.12 or later. - clang-format 22 if you contribute: `pip install clang-format==22.1.8`, the version CI runs. - Ghidra, optional, for reading functions nobody has written yet. See [docs/GHIDRA.md](docs/GHIDRA.md). - Your own copy of HyperBlade, with `HYPERX.EXE` at v1.0.0.1. ### Checking your copy Only v1.0.0.1 matches: | File | Size | MD5 | SHA256 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `HYPERX.EXE` | 860,160 | `420c5c49ee2ae5ae9adf329bb2ee5702` | `514bcec6805f27136bed6e4de8796e75d99f224a94e3d7098a4477b029ea24cd` | Check yours with: ```sh certutil -hashfile HYPERX.EXE SHA256 ``` A different hash usually means v1.0.0.0, the unpatched release. Install the 1.0.0.1 patch. ## Setup 1. Install the Python requirements, then patch reccmp: ```sh pip install -r tools/requirements.txt patch -p1 -d "$(python -c 'import os, reccmp; print(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(reccmp.__file__)))')" < tools/reccmp_call_table.patch ``` 2. Clone [zach2good/vc6-sp3-toolchain](https://github.com/zach2good/vc6-sp3-toolchain) and set `VC6_ROOT` to it. 3. Copy `reccmp-user.example.yml` to `reccmp-user.yml` and point it at your `HYPERX.EXE`. `python tools/reference.py` prints the path it found, or says what is missing. ## Build and score ```sh cmake --preset vc6sp3 cmake --build --preset vc6sp3 cmake --build build --target verify python -m reccmp.tools.asmcmp --target HYPERX --verbose 0xADDRESS --no-color ``` `verify` scores every function and runs the structural checks. The last line shows one function's diff. reccmp's `Dropped duplicate address` errors are expected. Don't run `build/out/HYPERX.exe`, which changes the display resolution. Without a copy of the game, configure with `-DHYPERX_NO_REFERENCE=ON`. That links `HYPERX_sym.exe` without the original's resources and runs no check. CI scores each pull request's image against a private copy of the original and reports the result on the pull request. ## Running the game The bring-up build adds a windowed mode and other fixes under `#ifdef HYPERX_BRINGUP`, and draws with the game's software renderer. Copy the disc's `DATA` folder into `build/out` as `Data`, then: ```sh cmake --preset bringup cmake --build --preset bringup python tools/check_match.py # play one match ``` To play by hand, run `build-bringup/out/hyperx_bringup_soft.exe`. `src/app/bringup.cpp` lists the `HB_` environment switches. ## Extracting the game's data ```sh python tools/extract_rc.py # menu, dialogs, strings, version and icon, as an .rc script python tools/extract_mdm1.py --png # every MDM1-packed bitmap in build/out/Data, as BMP and PNG python tools/plan_dump.py # the AI plans, printed as pseudo-source ``` The first two write under `build/extracted`. ## FAQ ### What does the percentage count? Bytes of game code below `0x004a0000` in functions that match exactly. Effective and partial matches count nothing. Some exact functions are libjpeg and C runtime code that matches because we link the same library. `python tools/progress.py` reports the share this project wrote by hand. ### Why Visual C++ 6.0 SP3? The original's Rich header names that toolchain, and only the same compiler and linker can emit the same bytes. `tools/richcheck.py` compares the two. ### Why match bytes instead of writing a port? A byte match proves the source is the program that shipped. Fixes and modernisation belong in [hyperblade-20XX](https://github.com/zach2good/hyperblade-20XX). ### Can I use AI tools? Yes, but review what they write closely. The project began as hand work and soon moved to AI tools under close human review. Point your tools at [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). The rules in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) apply to every change, whoever wrote it. ## Project structure | Path | What's in it | | --- | --- | | `src/` | The reconstructed source, one folder per subsystem. [src/README.md](src/README.md) lists them. | | `symbols/` | Facts about the original that the build and the checkers read. | | `tools/` | The scorer's helpers, the checkers and the extractors. [tools/README.md](tools/README.md) lists them. | | `docs/` | How the matching works, and what we've learned about the game. readme:
# Zombie Revenge decomp (kick-off)

A decompilation of the Dreamcast **Zombie Revenge**, in progress. It rebuilds the game's executable
byte for byte from one assembly file per function (the baseline the build keeps checking), with
1026 of its 4232 functions named so far. A function is **done** when its C behaves like the
original (Equivalent, checked by `tools/equiv.py`); byte-identical C (Matching) is the bonus tier.

**This repository contains no game code or data.** You supply your own disc; `setup.sh` generates
everything game-derived on your machine, and `.gitignore` keeps it out of git.

## Supported version

| | |
|---|---|
| Release | Zombie Revenge (Europe), MK-5103850, V1.000, 2000-02-09, area E |
| `1ST_READ.BIN` | 10299711 bytes, SHA-1 `aaa2a5cd6eb567fd0b44d7567c939318e5bed422` |
| Linked at | `0x0C010000` |
| SDK era | Katana SDK, mid-1999 (libraries closest to R1.55J; Shinobi 1.62zr, Kamui 1.11.0.1, ADXT 5.56, game-specific `zr` builds of pd, syHw, bu, kd, syInt) |

Other releases are different builds: `setup.sh` refuses them rather than produce a broken split.

## Building

You need: your own copy of the disc as a `.gdi` with its track files, Python 3, Docker, and a Katana SDK (its Hitachi
assembler and linker do the build; any folder layout works).

```
bash setup.sh "path/to/your disc.gdi"
echo 'SDK_PATH="/path/to/katana-sdk"' > .env      # once: where your SDK is (not committed)
bash build.sh
```

`build.sh` should end with `MATCH`. It builds its own small tools image the first time (Docker
must be running). The first build assembles every file (a few minutes); after
that only changed files. (Running the scripts with `bash` means file permissions never matter;
`./build.sh` works too once `setup.sh` has run.) Docker is required; on Linux x86_64 without
Docker, `DC_LOCAL=1` runs the tools through `wibo` instead.

## What is here

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `setup.sh` | Extract and verify your executable, generate `asm/`, `text-map/` and `model-map/` |
| `build.sh` | Assemble, link, convert, compare with your original |
| `disc.sh` | Build a playable disc image of your version (files you put under `disc/`) |
| `textures.sh` | Optional: every standard texture on one page, to look through |
| `BASE` | Link address |
| `functions.txt` | Every function: address, size, name (`FUN_<addr>` = not named yet) |
| `symbols.txt` | Addresses the C units use that no file defines yet (RAM, data inside asm) |
| `sdk.txt` | The bundled Sega SDK's code (for `tools/progress.py`) |
| `models.txt` | What is known about the game's 3D models: tables whose layout is understood (read by `tools/model_map.py`) |
| `src/` | C: Equivalent files (checked by `tools/equiv.py`, not built) and matching C units (built, see below) |
| `tests/` | Test cases per function (`tests/<file>/<function>.json`) and `tests/equivalent.txt`, the functions found Equivalent |
| `docs/equivalent.md` | The evidence for each Equivalent function (written by `tools/equiv.py`) |
| `sdk-verified.txt` | Library functions whose bytes the SDK source you supplied reproduces (written by `tools/sdk_source.py`) |
| `sdk-source/` | The C of those library functions, from the SDK source you supplied (local, git-ignored) |
| `AGENTS.md` | The per-function decompilation loop: Equivalent first, Matching as the bonus |
| `tools/` | Disc reader, splitter, text mapper, model mapper, C-unit layout, progress report, missed-function finder, SH-4 disassembler and simulator, the Equivalent check (`equiv.py`) with its helpers (`checksizes.py`, `classify.py`, `poollist.py`, `port_equiv.py`), the SDK-source check (`sdk_source.py`), live checks against the running game (optional) |

`text-map/` (generated) lists the executable's strings, how much text each disc file holds, and every image file
(`images.tsv`). Counts and lists for you to read, not a verdict.

## Model map

`setup.sh` also builds `model-map/game.dcgs` (with `tools/model_map.py`): every model it recognises in the disc files, the
table in the executable that holds it, the texture lists, every sound it recognises (CRI ADX and AHX streams, and the sound
banks), and, where a skeleton is known, characters assembled from their parts. It is plain tab-separated text in sections (`[models]`, `[assemblies]`, `[rigs]`, `[bones]`, `[audio]`, `[textures]`) and it is
**committed**: it holds addresses, offsets, sizes and names only, no game bytes or text (the text map is the one
that stays local). Regenerate it with `python3 tools/model_map.py 1ST_READ.BIN "$(cat BASE)" functions.txt "<your disc>.gdi" model-map`.

- **No setup needed to start.** With no rules the map still lists every model it recognises, grouped by the table that holds it.
- **`models.txt` is what is known about the game's models**, one rule per line: `chars` and `structs` (tables whose
  layout is understood), `rig` / `bone` / `assemble` (a skeleton posed from a motion record), `nodes` / `nodelayout` (linked node structs in
  the executable, each character placed in its bind pose), `textures` (pairs a
  model file with a texture file of another name; matching names are found by themselves), `note`, and the two a
  person adds by naming things: `name <file> <offset> <text>` (one model), `sound <file> <entry> <text>` (one sound), `image <file> <offset> <text>` (one picture) and `table <address> <group> <label>`
  (a whole table). The syntax is in the header of `tools/model_map.py`.
- **Naming convention.** A row shows the name first and the id beside it, and only the id when there is no name.
  Names are tidied the same way everywhere: words separated by single spaces (underscores and camelCase become
  spaces), each word starting with a capital, no parentheses. Ids (hex offsets, table addresses, the game's own
  identifiers) are never changed.
- **Naming things.** Edit `models.txt` and rerun the tool, or use a model viewer that opens this folder and writes
  the `name` and `table` lines for you, into two sorted blocks at the end of the file, so a naming session is a small
  `git diff`. Commit the diff.

## Equivalent C and shared library code

`src/<file>.c` with no `@unit` header is C checked for behaviour only: `python3 tools/equiv.py src/<file>.c`
runs each function in an SH-4 interpreter twice per test case, the original bytes and your compiled C,
and they must agree on calls, memory writes and the result. Passing functions are listed in
`tests/equivalent.txt` and counted as done. The loop, and how to write many of them quickly, is in
`AGENTS.md` and the kickoff skill's `references/equivalent-pipeline.md`. Library code the game shares
with another decomp of this skill (the NAOMI library, the C runtime) need not be rewritten:
`python3 tools/port_equiv.py <that decomp> .` finds those functions here by their code, ports the C and
its cases, and keeps only what `equiv.py` confirms on this game's own bytes.

## Matching C units (the build tier)

A file `src/<name>.c` whose first line is `/* @unit <start>-<end> [shc options] */` replaces every
asm file in that address range. `build.sh` compiles it with the SDK's `shc` to assembly, lays it
out exactly like the original (`tools/fill.py`: alignment as nops, reserved gaps as `0xEE`, padded
to `<end>`), assembles it and links it in place; the result still has to `MATCH`. A unit with
constant data (initialised local arrays, const tables, string literals) also names where the
original link put that data: `/* @unit <start>-<end> @data <dstart>-<dend> [shc options] */`. The
data becomes its own piece at that range, in source order; both ranges must start and end on asm
file boundaries (add them to `functions.txt`: `F <addr> 0 FUN_<addr>` for a function start,
`D <addr> 0 data_<addr>` for a data boundary, which is not counted as a function). A unit is one
original source file: all its functions share literal pools, so it goes in only when all of it
matches. `python3 tools/progress.py` reports the state,
each function in one bucket: done (equivalent C; matching C and SDK source part of it), named only (a name is
not done work), unnamed; plus documented functions and named globals. `docs/equivalent.md` holds
the evidence for each equivalent function.

## Progress

<!-- progress -->
```
THE GAME                          4232 functions, 673196 bytes of code; each function in one bucket
  done: equivalent C        6.5%  273 of 4232 functions, 15034 bytes (2.2%): C that behaves like the original
    of which matching C     0.0%  0 functions, 0 bytes, 0 units: rebuilt byte for byte
    of which SDK source     6.5%  273 functions, 15034 bytes: the SDK's own source reproduces them (sdk-source/, local)
  named only               17.8%  753 functions: a name, no C yet (not done work)
  unnamed                  75.8%  3206 functions (FUN_...), no C yet
  documented                0.0%  0 named functions in docs/*.md
  named globals                   0
  of which library                588 functions, 83572 bytes of code: the Sega SDK, the NAOMI library and the C runtime bundled in the game
    done                   21.9%  129 of 588 library functions, 9878 bytes (11.8%)
    named                 100.0%  588 of 588 (the library's own names, from SDK tables)
```
<!-- /progress -->

Updated on every commit by `tools/hooks/pre-commit` (enable once per clone:
`git config core.hooksPath tools/hooks`).

## Names

Names come from signature matching: 997 matches from the Katana SDK's own libraries (only
unique matches are applied). 1026
functions carry a name in all, because small wrappers inherit the name of the function they call.

## How this was started

This repo was autogenerated using
[dc-decomp-kickoff](https://github.com/consolesplayingconsoles/dc-decomp-kickoff) v0.6+4791a9e.

## Third-party sources

The build needs a Katana SDK. Repositories that hold such material (for example
`Kochise/dreamcast-docs`)
are named solely as examples of the type of material required. We have no affiliation with, and
make no representation regarding, those repositories, their contents, or their licensing. You are
solely responsible for determining whether you are entitled to obtain and use any such material.

Zombie Revenge and its publisher's trademarks belong to their owners. This project is not affiliated with
or endorsed by them.

readme:
# Street Fighter III 3rd Strike - CPS3 program source

**AI Disclosure**:
Yes, this used Claude, decompiling compilers is thirsty work.
It also used the hard manual work from https://github.com/crowded-street/3s-decomp which was hand built, and I have discussed that fact with them with approval.
The PS2 Debug disk of the Anniversary provided the layout, and names of most of what is in here and the 3s-decomp, and the names of the files here are what Capcom named their files, so blame them for Eff18.c etc.

It has been in the works for a number of months / years, and relies on the work of collaborators who know 3rd Strike inside out. 

Right, back to it.

C and SH-2 assembler source for the CPS3 program ROM of *Street Fighter III 3rd Strike: Fight for the Future*
(sfiii3nr1), built with the original Hitachi toolchain (SHC 5.0, asmsh, lnk 6.0, rof2bin). PS2 was used as a reference only, it is 100% Arcade logic and code.

The build is a working program, not a byte-for-byte copy of the arcade ROM as matching is in the final stages: code and data are laid out by the
linker from this source.

## Building

Needs Windows (the tools in `bin/` are Win32 programs) and Python 3.

1. Put your `sfiii3nr1.zip` in `rom/`.
2. Run `build.bat` (or `make`).

The build reads the graphics pattern tables from the ROM (they are not in this source), compiles and links the
program, and writes:

- `build/prog.bin` - the program image, 06000000-06FFFFFF
- `build/sfiii3nr1.zip` - your ROM set with the two program SIMMs replaced

`build/prog.bin` should match the SHA-1 in `tools/prog.sha1`; the build prints whether it does.

When running a new build in MAME, use an empty `-nvram_directory`: MAME keeps the program SIMMs' flash in nvram
and loads it over the ROM files.

## Layout

    src/      game code (C, and SH-2 assembler in .src files)
    data/     game tables
    include/  headers
    lib/      the compiler's run-time routines, as linked into the program
    bin/      Hitachi SHC toolchain (four stages rebuilt, see below; the originals are in bin/original)
    sf3.sub   link order and section addresses
    functions.tsv  every routine of the arcade program: arcade address, size, name, file
    tools/    cps3rom.py: reads the ROM set, writes the new one

## Compiler

The compiler is SHC 5.0 Release 26 with thirty-nine changes, each one a rule the arcade's own compiler visibly follows
throughout the ROM but Release 26 doesn't:

- a switch case is tested with `bt case` / `bra default` (Release 26 folds it into `bf default`), and a jump whose
  target has become the next block is kept as a `bra` to the next instruction: the jump to a case or default
  label, the jump over an else arm that was merged with a later identical block, the jump in front of
  `else return;` (Release 26 deletes every such jump; only the one a then arm makes over `else break;` still goes);
- two returns share the instructions they end with only as far back as those leave r0 alone: the store or call
  in front of a plain `return;`, never the `mov #0,r0` of `return 0;` (Release 26 shares every instruction they
  end with), and an instruction that uses r0 does not fill the delay slot of the jump to the shared code; inside
  a `switch`, a return whose whole block would be shared keeps its own copy; and once returns were shared the
  function keeps its epilogue and `rts`, even when every path now ends in a tail call; it keeps them too when
  the only jump to them was in code that could not be reached and was removed (`if (c) f(); else g(); break;`
  at the end of a function);
- a constant loaded into r0 is loaded again after a conditional branch (Release 26 carries it across);
- a stack load or store never fills a branch delay slot;
- a value that is only tested takes the lowest free register (Release 26 starts from r3);
- constants passed to calls count when deciding which values to keep in a register;
- `sts macl` is never scheduled ahead of the multiply it reads (a Release 26 scheduling fault), so array indexing
  can be written plainly;
- a branch is not threaded through a label that merging identical code created;
- a narrow value multiplied by a 16-bit constant uses `mul.l`, not `muls.w`, and a `short` is extended
  (`exts.w`) before that multiply;
- an integer cast of a table's name, `(u32)table`, is loaded again at each use rather than kept across calls;
- `f(&p->first)`, with `first` at offset 0, counts as passing `p`, so `p` can stay in its argument register;
- a global variable is loaded again at each use, not read from a copy an earlier use kept in a register or on the stack;
  the same goes for an expression several branches compute, when the first of them can't share its value, and
  for the uses a call or store cuts off from the first: only the uses reached from the first share its value;
- after a multiply the multiplier counts as busy for one instruction, not two, so `sts macl` can follow the next load;
  and that one instruction is the first that is ready, in either half of a long word (Release 26 keeps memory
  accesses to the first half there too, so it would take a literal load ahead of a register move);
- a switch's compare-and-branch jumps leave r1 free, so a value live into the cases can move into it and r13/r14 is not saved;
- a load through a pointer and a later separate `add` to the pointer stay apart (Release 26 folds them into a
  post-increment load, `mov.w @r5+,r0`); the arcade has post-increments only where the source has `*p++`;
  likewise an `add` of minus the size to a pointer and a store through it stay apart (Release 26 folds them into
  a pre-decrement store), so `*--p = x` is `mov.l r1,@-r4` only while `p` is used again;
- a `char` cast of a loop counter's multiple, `(char)(i * 6)`, still counts as a multiple of the counter, so the
  value steps by 6 on each pass instead of being multiplied again (a cast to `short` is still recomputed, as in the arcade);
- a structure copied in a loop that counts down, `a[i] = a[i - 1]`, is copied first and its pointers are stepped
  after the copy (Release 26 makes the destination a pre-decrement access, which a block move can't use, so the
  pointer starts one element further on and is stepped before each copy);
- in the files compiled without optimization, a load or store of a local variable counts as 4 bytes, not 6, when
  the compiler decides where a literal pool goes, so those pools come later;
- a `for` or `while` loop is entered by a jump to its test at the bottom (Release 26, asked for speed, puts a copy
  of the test in front of nearly every loop instead); only a loop with no loop inside it, whose test compares two
  local variables or constants, gets the copy;
- the last use of a variable kept on the stack reads it from the stack again, even straight after the store
  (Release 26 takes it from the register the value was computed in); earlier uses still take the register;
- once an array's address is loaded, the scratch register that held an earlier address or constant counts as
  free again (Release 26 goes on avoiding it), so the next value is loaded into it;
- a `short` or `char` index whose first use is scaled (`shorts[ix]`) is extended again at each `chars[ix]`
  (Release 26 extends it once for the byte arrays and keeps that copy in a register across branches);
- a multiply reads a constant that is already in a register: a `char` or `short` multiply takes it from there
  (`muls.w r12,r3`, where Release 26 shifts), and the 16-bit constant of an `int` multiply of a `char` or `short`
  counts like any other, so `s * 100` used three times keeps 100 in a register (Release 26 loads it at each multiply);
- when an address is the sum of a pointer still in memory (a row of a table of pointers, `table[a]` in
  `table[a][b]`) and an index in a register, the pointer is loaded and added (`mov.l @(r0,r3),r3`, `add r3,r2`,
  `mov.l @r2,r1`); Release 26 loads it into r0 and indexes with it; the same holds when the other part of the
  sum is the address of a table or is already in r0, and for a fixed offset from an address the compiler itself
  keeps on the stack: the address is loaded and the offset added;
- an index used by several arrays in one statement stays in its own register, and each access takes its array's
  address into r0 or adds (Release 26 copies the index into r0 once and uses every array as a base);
- a zero that is added or subtracted (the index of `a[0]`) and the constant of a bit-and (`v & 3`) or of a
  bit-xor (`p->flag ^ 1`) count when a constant is weighed for a register, and read the register that holds it (Release 26 passes over every use that
  can be an immediate); so do a constant added to or subtracted from a local variable (`(ix + 1) & 1`) and the
  constant of `+=` and `-=`, while a constant added to a value just read from memory (`p->m + 1`) stays an immediate;
- a zero compared unsigned with a converted value (`i < n` with `unsigned i` and `int n`, in the test in front of
  a loop where `i` is still 0) is not an immediate: the SH has no unsigned compare with an immediate, so the zero
  is kept in a register and the compare reads that register (`cmp/hs r10,r4`); Release 26 goes by the type of the
  comparison itself, which is always a signed `int`, takes the zero for an immediate and copies its register
  first (`mov r4,r3`, `cmp/hs r10,r3`). Only one routine shows this, `strstr`;
- a mask by 0xff, `x & 0xFF` or `v &= 0xFF`, stays an `and` (Release 26 turns it into a cast, so the code
  extends with `extu.b`); `extu.b` comes from a cast or an `unsigned char`;
- in a loop, the address of a member reached through a pointer, `p->a`, is not taken as fixed when stepping
  pointers are made, so for `p->a[i]` only `i * size` steps (Release 26 makes the element's address a pointer
  that steps by the element size);
- a value derived from the loop counter and used more than once (`i * 2`, or `&a[i]` used by two statements)
  gets a new stepping variable, and the shared copy is taken from it on each pass (`mov r4,r7`); Release 26
  steps the shared copy itself. An address that another argument of the same call takes again
  (`f(a[i].x, a[i].y)`) or that one test uses twice, and an address a later statement uses while the counter
  counts down, keep Release 26's choice, and the index of a `char` array is extended on each pass instead of stepped;
- the scratch register a `break` or `continue` picks for its jump is not counted as in use by the statement in
  front of it, so a value that is live there can still move into that register at the end of the function and
  r8-r14 need not be saved for it (Release 26 counts it);
- when every use of an `int` loop counter has become a stepping pointer, the counter is dropped and the loop's
  test compares one of the pointers with the end of the table (`cmp/hs r14,r4`); Release 26 holds the code for
  this but no option switches it on, so it keeps the counter beside the pointers;
- the index of a `char` array that is read from memory (`flags[p->id]`, `cols[src[i]]`) is the converted value
  itself, so `flags[p->id] &= 0x80` keeps the index in r0, loads the array's address once, reads through it
  indexed and copies it for the store; Release 26 takes the index for a second value, copies it out of r0 and
  loads the address twice; a `char` or `short` variable used as such an index is taken the same way, unless its
  first use as an index in the function is the test of an `if`;
- an expression used in several blocks is shared even when it holds a temporary: with `table[ix]` read in
  several places the element address is computed once in front of its uses; Release 26 leaves such an
  expression alone, shares only the index and adds the table's address again at each use;
- a switch's comparison chain reuses the selector register r0 for a possible far jump to a case or default,
  where the selector is no longer needed, and records that use before restoring each case's register state.
  Release 26 uses r1, which also prevents preceding instructions that use r1 from filling some delay slots;
- byte and short integer sums reuse a constant already held in a register. Release 26 reserves that constant
  for a possible address displacement even though its address-folding pass excludes these narrow results.
  Wide integers and address calculations keep the original decision;
- an indexed word store loads its displacement before a constant OR when the prepared register operation
  leaves r0 untouched; calls, stack effects, volatile stores and r0 results keep the original order;
- a switch's jump table does not reset the short reach a word constant in front of it gave the next literal
  pool, so the pool behind the table comes sooner (Release 26 starts over with the long reach);
- when the place of a literal pool is worked out, a `return` in a function that saves one register and MACL
  is not counted as needing the exit's address as a literal (Release 26 counts MACH and MACL among the saved
  registers there, and with two or more a `return` is a jump that may need one).

The four changed stages (`shcmdl.exe`, `shcgen.exe`, `shcpep.exe` and `shcasm.exe`) are rebuilt from a C
decompilation of the originals (source: https://github.com/gibletto/shc-5r26-decomp-sf3), and each rule is a
setting in that source (thirty-nine settings for the thirty-nine rules: the switch rule and the return rule have two each, the `char` cast rule and the structure copy rule share `MDL_IV`, and the unsigned zero rule shares `MDL_IMM_REG` with the rule for constants that are added, masked or xored). With every rule off they give the same output as Release 26. Setting `SWITCH_ARCADE_BRANCH`,
`SWITCH_ARCADE_JUMP`, `XJUMP_OFF`, `PEP_R0_FORGET`, `SLOT_NO_STACK`, `PEP_NO_THREAD`, `GEN_TST_R0`, `GEN_MUL_L`,
`MDL_ARG_CONST`, `MDL_CAST_CSE`, `MDL_ARG_CAST`, `MDL_GCSE`, `ASM_MULWAIT`, `GEN_CHAIN_JUMP`, `GEN_CHAIN_SCRATCH_R0`, `GEN_NARROW_CONST`, `GEN_OR_INDEX_EARLY`, `PEP_AUTOINC`, `MDL_IV`, `GEN_POOL_MOVLOC`, `MDL_LOOP_INV`, `GEN_RELOAD`, `GEN_EVICT_ORDER`, `MDL_CAST_MUL`, `MDL_MUL_CONST`, `PEP_RET_R0`, `GEN_MEM_INDEX`, `GEN_R0VAR`, `MDL_IMM_REG`, `MDL_MASK_AND`, `MDL_IV_BASE`, `MDL_IV_TEMP`, `GEN_JUMP_TEMP`, `MDL_TEST_REPLACE`, `MDL_MUL_ONE`, `MDL_TEMP_EXPR`, `PEP_CASE_WORD`, `PEP_RET_MAC` and `ASM_SPECREG` to 0 gives Release 26's behaviour back. The
original files are in `bin/original`.

With the changes, 9,982 of the 10,066 C routines compile to the arcade's instructions (3,811 with the original
Release 26), and 9,974 to its exact bytes (1,912). Fightcade replays are kept as a sanity check and were last run
on the build of 16 October 2026: of 254 replays compared with the original ROM, all 254 kept identical game state
throughout (218 before) and identical slowdown (214).

## Fightcade replays

Fightcade replays can't be played on this build out of the box. A replay is an FBNeo savestate taken on the real
ROM plus the inputs for each frame. Work RAM and the ROM tables are at the same addresses in this build, but the
code isn't. The saved CPU state, task stacks and function pointers all point into arcade code, so loading the
savestate as is will crash.

You'd need a custom FBNeo build that can:

- run the replay on the original ROM and save a state once the scheduler (`Game_Task`) is idle, so no task is
  halfway through a function;
- load that state into this build with a patch applied (registers and RAM words), then carry on feeding the
  replay's inputs from that frame.

Making the patch is the fiddly part:

- `functions.tsv` gives each routine's arcade address and `sf3.map` gives where it ended up, so any code address
  in the state can be mapped by name.
- Restart the scheduler at `Game_Task` on its boot stack, and point each task's function slot at the new address.
- If a sleeping task's function is just a loop around its sleep call, restart it at its entry. Otherwise fix up
  its saved return address and whatever registers the new code expects to survive the call.
- Some words in the initialised data (the part copied from ROM at boot) still hold arcade code addresses. Swap
  those for the new ones. If anything else in RAM looks like a code address, check it by hand.

To compare the two runs, hash the game variables every logic frame (not every video frame) and treat code
addresses as zero, since they'll always differ. Expect the odd drift where the arcade drops a frame and this build
doesn't. The code doesn't take exactly the same cycles yet, so that's timing, not a logic bug.

## Thanks

Thanks to the 3sx Team and Artem for the 3s-decomp, which helped recover a large amount of this code style, and to
DrewDos for his matching work and help.

Doing that by hand, alone, would take many years. With AI tools it becomes possible. AI writes the first drafts, but nothing is accepted on its word: every function is checked byte for byte with the original compiler, and after every change the whole game is rebuilt and compared with the retail executable. To everyone else who loves this game as much as I do: welcome, and thank you for being here. ## Status **Active, started in October 2026.** The source code is not public yet. readme:
# Vagrant Story native/dynarec port

This repository targets the USA PlayStation release of **Vagrant Story**
(`SLUS_010.40`) as a native/dynarec hybrid built on
[psxport](https://github.com/SomeoneIsWorking/psxport). The player supplies the original disc; no
game content is distributed here.

## Current status

The dynarec title adapter exists and `./run.sh` builds and launches the `vagrant_port` product, which
executes the authenticated resident image and reached `.PRG` overlays through psxport's per-`Core`
Lightrec executor. There is no interpreter fallback, no engine selector, and no generated guest
corpus; `tools/verify.py` inspects the shipped binary's symbols to keep that true.

**The title boots from the real disc into BATTLE, but it is not yet playable end to end.** A New Game runs the
resident boot, TITLE (splashes, intro movie, menu) and the BATTLE prologue under psxport's dynarec; the `warp
<save point>` control command loads a map into free roam through the game's own location transition. Later
overlays, saves and progression are unverified; save point 1 faults (`docs/issues/0052`).

Title-owned work: authenticated resident and `.PRG` provisioning, finite resident/TITLE phases, CD and
memory-card ownership, pad delivery, native heap behaviour, the BATTLE culls that admit 16:9 margins, and the
measured retail facts each rests on. See `docs/project-state.md` for the capability inventory, `docs/issues/`
for open defects, and `docs/re-frontier.md` for the ordered binary evidence chain.

## Intended product

- Execute every non-native guest instruction on demand through psxport's per-Core Lightrec runtime.
- Never link, select, or fall back to an interpreter in gameplay; a separate test oracle is allowed.
- Preserve authenticated resident/overlay image identity and invalidate translated blocks when a
  reused `.PRG` slot changes generation.
- Keep deliberately native CD, save, input, timing, and rendering owners behind image-scoped
  overrides with original calls routed through the dynarec.
- Reach representative interactive BATTLE gameplay before claiming compatibility.
- Add semantic native world rendering, true widescreen, and presentation interpolation only after
  the faithful baseline is verified.

## Developer entry points

The launcher remains the stable player interface:

```sh
./run.sh
```

It provisions the authenticated measured inputs, configures, builds `vagrant_port`, and launches it.
`./run.sh --prepare-only` does everything except the launch, which opens a window and plays audio.
Help remains available with `./run.sh --help`. Focused migration checks do not use the launcher:

```sh
CXX=clang++ uv run --frozen python tools/verify.py
uv run --frozen python tools/extract_exe.py /path/to/disc.chd
uv run --frozen python tools/extract_overlays.py /path/to/disc.chd
```

The extraction commands place authenticated runtime inputs under gitignored `scratch/`. The normal
verifier configures a Ninja build under `build/verify`, builds and runs the native image/title
contracts AND the shipping product, inspects that product's symbols to prove no interpreter is
linked, checks first-party C++ with clang-format and clang-tidy, then runs the Python tests and
structure policy. It checks the Python launcher composition and its stage-named refusals, exact-image
provisioning behavior, the 1,200-line source cap, Python-only automation, absence of retired
execution dependencies, and product-code bans on direct stderr and process-environment reads.

The eventual fresh-clone product requires `uv`, CMake, Git, a C++20 compiler, and psxport's documented
native dependencies. Maintainer C++ verification uses Clang, clang-format, and clang-tidy; the shipped
project remains compatible with its supported GCC, Clang, and AppleClang toolchains.

## Legal

The disc image, extracted executable, and overlays remain user-owned and gitignored. The vendored CC0
`rood-reverse` decompilation is a readable source aid for the exact game revision, not independent
runtime evidence. The shared `go-public` skill's `go_public.py` (under
`~/repo/shared/re-harness/tools/`, not vendored here) audits repository history for game-derived
content and machine-specific paths.

readme:
# Toy Story 2 native/dynarec port

This repository targets the USA PlayStation release of *Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue!*
(`SLUS_008.93`). It combines title-owned native subsystems with psxport's runtime Lightrec executor;
the authenticated user-supplied game image remains data.

## Current state

The durable feature inventory and exact gaps are in [project-state](docs/project-state.md), and the
open product bugs are in [docs/issues](docs/issues).

The Linux x86-64 product links against psxport's maintained Lightrec executor and runs the title,
menu, level select, LEVEL01 and Andy's Room through it. Native boundary tests pass; native scene
producers and true widescreen for the front end remain open. No offline guest source or
player-selectable interpreter path is present.

## Build and run

Provide the original disc through `PSXPORT_TS2_DISC`, `.env`, an unambiguous repository-root CHD, or
the optional positional argument:

```sh
./run.sh [/path/to/game.chd]
```

`run.sh` is only the launcher. It resolves psxport, configures `build/player`, builds
`build/player/bin/toystory2_port`, and starts that product. It does not run tests or generate guest
code.

The gate is build + the product's hermetic C++ boundary tests + the executable's own help contract +
clang-format/clang-tidy/cpp_policy:

```sh
CXX=clang++ CC=clang CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=6 uv run --frozen python tools/verify.py
```

`tools/verify.py` uses psxport's shared consumer verifier to configure the Ninja
`build/verify` tree, build the product, run that CTest suite, and inspect the linked execution
boundary. Maintained dependency overrides use `PSXPORT_LIGHTREC_DIR` and
`PSXPORT_LIGHTNING_PREFIX`, matching the framework verifier. This asset-free check does not establish
gameplay compatibility.

To look at the game, drive it, or capture frames, use the maintainer tool: `tools/headless_run.py`
(one bounded headless run of `--frames` presentation-fence steps, with `--tap` for an exact-frame schedule, `--pad` to replay a recorded
phase-keyed `replays/*.pad`, `--shot-at`, `--aspect`, `--dump-at`). `--tap` schedules exact-frame
probes for one live session; what must keep working over time is a recording, because an absolute
schedule assumes how many pad frames boot and the movies consume. It is not part of the gate.

Game files, extracted executables, build products, and runtime captures are not tracked or packaged.

metadata.description: Evidence-backed decompilation of Larax & Zaco (LEZAC.EXE) using REA and Ghidra

readme:
# Lezac decompilation

Evidence-backed reverse engineering of **Larax & Zaco v1.0 shareware**
(`LEZAC.EXE`), using [REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea) **6.3.0** and
Ghidra **12.1.4**.

**Status: 215 default-discovered procedures exported; seven routines reconstructed
in original-style Pascal, sixteen packed storage layouts, and the prior six C
reconstructions. Native differential tests and a rebuilt 16-bit DOS computational
probe pass. The ORIGINAL game has a pinned DOSBox-X reference baseline, with level 1
completed under it. This is NOT a playable rebuild, a bit-identical rebuild, or the
author's original source files.**

## What is here

- [Original-style Pascal recovery](docs/pascal-recovery.md): six core routines
  plus the legacy RLE decompressor, with **174,777 native Pascal-versus-original
  comparisons**. A separate compiled i8086 MZ probe executes all seven operations
  in a limited DOS-service fixture and compares twelve original invocations.
- [Sixteen packed-record layouts](pascal/LZTYPES.PAS), compiled and measured on
  native and DOS targets: actors, animation, debris, scores and resource records.
  Names are inferred; unknown bytes are preserved. Exact author syntax and
  compiler version are not recovered.
- **215 function dossiers, 215 C-like pseudocode files and 215 assembly files**
  under [`analysis/rea/verified/`](analysis/rea/verified/). They retain REA Evidence
  IDs, input identity, inclusive body ranges, calls, references and limitations.
- **94 successful loaded-image checks**, including the original file mapping and
  DOS relocation processing. Input SHA-256:
  `7579255148c2cb540b26f70dc8181c50b218b6808d8fa5208c832391bafa53ec`.
- [Six portable C routines](recovered/lezac.c): checksum, animation initialization,
  wrapping add/clamp, friction, state initialization and tile collection.
  **173,725 C-versus-original x86 cases**, including every signed 16-bit friction
  input; the same cases pass with GCC's undefined-behavior sanitizer.
- **29 additional original-code decompressor probes** characterize source
  overread and overlapping extra stores without patching game instructions.
- Resource-format research and strict decoders for sprites, palette, scores,
  sound records and level containers. All 250 sprites and seven level records
  are accounted for; uncertain level tails are reported rather than invented.
- Pinned input provenance, a verified original-file importer, repeatable REA
  exporter, coverage index, tests, and CI.
- [Byte-decoded assembly audit](analysis/segment-register-audit.json): 23 reversed
  operand presentations among 65 checked register-direct segment MOVs. The raw
  REA export is unchanged; original executable bytes take precedence.
- [Original-game emulator baseline](docs/emulator-baseline.md): a hash-pinned
  DOSBox-X 2024.03.01 with a fixed configuration. `tools/run_original.py` runs the
  authenticated original from disposable copies, records input traces and exact VGA
  framebuffer checkpoints, and re-verifies the originals after every run. The
  committed run summaries cover a level-1 completion, death and restart, and
  two-player controls. Gameplay replays are host-timed, not cycle-exact.

Original EXE/ZIP/resource files and generated image previews are **not committed**.
See [RIGHTS.md](RIGHTS.md); archival availability is not a public-domain claim.

## Start here

- [Original-game emulator baseline: setup, observed behavior, level inventory](docs/emulator-baseline.md)
- [Pascal recovery, build targets, verification and limits](docs/pascal-recovery.md)
- [Pascal core contracts and original calling conventions](docs/pascal-core.md)
- [Record layouts, static links and compiler/source archaeology](docs/pascal-layouts.md)
- [Analysis, function roles and limitations](docs/analysis.md)
- [Reproduction instructions and tool versions](docs/reproduction.md)
- [Recovered C: original ABI, exact behavior and test domains](docs/recovered-routines.md)
- [Resource formats and the level-decoder defect](docs/resource-formats.md)
- [Machine-readable input/tool provenance](analysis/provenance.json)
- [All 215 functions as CSV](analysis/functions.csv)
- [Coverage measurements](analysis/coverage.json)

Raw decompiler `.c` files are intentionally **not compiled**. They contain
Ghidra pseudotypes, imperfect signatures and preserved warnings; the separate
`recovered/` directory is the actual compilable C subset.

## Quick verification

Requires Python 3.12+, a C99 compiler, Free Pascal 3.2.2, make, Node.js compatible
with REA, and npm. DOS tests additionally need the i8086 cross compiler; see the
Pascal build instructions above. Missing optional cross tooling is reported as
a skip, not as a passing DOS validation.

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
npm ci
python tools/fetch_original.py
make all
make pascal-native PYTHON=python
make test PYTHON=python
LEZAC_CFLAGS='-fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all' \
  python -m pytest tests/test_recovered.py -q
```

`make all` produces `build/liblezac.a` and `build/liblezac.so`, not a game
executable. The importer can use `--archive /path/to/lezac.zip` for an offline
copy; it validates every original file and refuses to overwrite different files.
With the cross compiler configured, `make pascal-dos PYTHON=python` builds and
executes `LZPROBE.EXE`. This is a new verification harness, not `LEZAC.EXE`.

To rerun REA after installing Ghidra and a full JDK:

```sh
export GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR=/absolute/path/to/ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC
export JAVA_HOME=/absolute/path/to/jdk-21
export GHIDRA_HEADLESS_MAXMEM=768M
export REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS=180000
mkdir -p build
node tools/analyze.mjs original/game/LEZAC.EXE build/rea-new
```

Use a new output directory. The exporter processes the whole discovered
inventory and fails on missing results. Oversized MCP responses are recovered
from their exact retained Evidence records, not truncated.

## What remains

- Recover dynamic targets such as the registered timer and keyboard interrupt
  handlers; **215 discovered routines is not proof of exhaustive code discovery**.
- Resolve remaining actor/map field meanings and reconstruct complete parent
  routines, physics, rendering, audio, input and DOS services; then test gameplay.
- Establish actual heap/buffer state for the missing tails of all fourteen
  compressed level planes. A safe decoder must not silently reproduce the
  original out-of-bounds accesses or fabricate replacement bytes.
- Make original-game replays cycle-exact and capture machine state. The pinned
  DOSBox-X delivers input in host time, and its save states abort while the game
  holds a file open. Both need a separately pinned, patched emulator (see the
  emulator baseline).

CI checks evidence integrity and the reconstructed subset. It does not make the
unreconstructed remainder correct, and it does not rerun Ghidra on every push.
